summary.title: Writing a Linux Debugger: Part 6 - Source-level stepping
summary.one_liner: You learn how to implement step-in, step-over, and step-out in a C/C++ debugger on Linux by combining ptrace single-stepping, temporary breakpoints, and DWARF line table data.
keywords: set breakpoint at every line in function
takeaways: Single-step instruction support (stepi) is built from PTRACE_SINGLESTEP, with a wrapper that temporarily disables breakpoints at the current PC.
Step out is implemented by reading the return address at rbp+8 and running until a temporary breakpoint there is hit.
Step in is a loop of instruction single-steps until the DWARF line number changes.
Step over is a naive approach: place temporary breakpoints on every line-table entry in the current function (except the current line) plus the return address, then continue.
The author notes the approach is simplified: it may step over breakpoints accidentally, and stepping out of main or into dynamically linked libraries may break.
summary.summary: This post, part 6 of a series on writing a Linux debugger, adds source-level stepping on top of earlier work with DWARF line information. It first exposes instruction-level stepping (stepi) with a breakpoint-aware wrapper, then implements step_out by setting a temporary breakpoint at the return address, step_in by single-stepping until the source line changes, and step_over by placing temporary breakpoints on all line-table addresses within the current function. The author deliberately uses naive approaches, acknowledging limitations such as possible accidental breakpoint stepping, and suggests a test program with nested function calls to exercise the commands.
